analysis.one_liner: Bans political action committees from federal elections and caps individual candidate contributions at $100.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the House with no cosponsors, sent to the House Administration Committee, and never received a vote before the 103rd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite campaign finance law in two ways. It would prohibit political action committees (PACs) — the committees funded by corporations, unions, and trade associations — from contributing to or spending on federal elections. It would also cut the limit on what an individual can give to a candidate from $1,000 to $100 per election. The goal is to make campaigns run on many small individual donations instead of organized money pools.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters and candidates who lack access to PAC money. With PACs barred from federal elections and individual gifts capped at $100, candidates would have to raise money from many small donors, giving everyday citizens more relative weight in funding elections and reducing the leverage that corporate, union, and trade-association committees hold over members of Congress.

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds a section to the Federal Election Campaign Act stating that no person other than an individual or a political committee may make contributions, solicit or receive contributions, or make expenditures to influence a federal election, effectively cutting PACs out of federal campaigns.
The bill reduces the ceiling on candidate contributions by persons other than multicandidate political committees from $1,000 to $100, shrinking the weight of any single large donor.

analysis.who_pays: PACs and the corporations, unions, and trade associations that fund them lose their channel into federal elections, and candidates and party committees that rely on PAC money would have to rebuild fundraising around small individual gifts.
analysis.who_pays_short: PACs and their corporate and union sponsors

drawbacks.text: The bill only bars contributions and expenditures made 'for the purpose of influencing an election for Federal office' and does not address money given to political parties or spent in other channels, so organized money could be redirected rather than eliminated.

A $100 individual contribution limit is far tighter than the existing $1,000 limit; candidates would need many times more donors to raise the same money, and some analysts argue such low limits can advantage wealthy candidates who can fund their own campaigns.
The bill drew no cosponsors, so even supporters of campaign finance reform in the House did not attach their names to this version.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets the core mechanism by which organized money reaches federal candidates — PAC contributions and spending — and would shift campaigns toward small donations, a clear gain for voters relative to PAC sponsors. Its main weaknesses are that it leaves side channels open and sets a very low individual limit that could create new problems. It never advanced far enough for those trade-offs to be debated on the floor.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on February 3, 1993 and referred to the House Administration Committee, which never took it up; it sat there until the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995 without a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Romano Mazzoli introduced the bill on February 3, 1993.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on House Administration on the day it was introduced, and the action history shows no further action, markup, or vote.
The 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995, and the bill expired in committee without receiving a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: PACs and the corporate, union, and trade-association interests that fund them kept their access to federal elections, and incumbents kept the PAC fundraising system that benefits sitting members. Nothing changed for voters, because the bill never received a vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: PACs and their sponsors, plus incumbents

for.name: Rep. Romano L. Mazzoli
for.role: U.S. Representative from Kentucky; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban PACs from federal elections and cut the individual contribution limit to $100.

against.name: House Committee on House Administration
against.role: Committee of referral; never scheduled action on the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on February 3, 1993 and took no further action, leaving it to die at the end of the 103rd Congress.

against.name: House colleagues of Rep. Mazzoli
against.what_they_did: No member joined as a cosponsor during the bill's two years on the books.

sides.party_line_note: With zero cosponsors, the record shows only a single Democratic sponsor and no visible support or opposition from either party; the bill never reached a vote where party splits could be measured.

industries.industry: Political action committees (corporate, labor, and trade-association PACs)
industries.note: The bill would have barred PACs entirely from federal elections and cut the individual contribution limit to $100, removing the main organized-money channel into congressional campaigns. Because the bill died in committee, PACs retained their role and revenue stream unchanged.

The firms and interest groups that operate PACs and cultivate member access keep the system the bill would have dismantled. The bill's failure means the status quo — access tied to organized contributions — remained in place.
